feign

FAYN -- from Latin fingere ('to shape, form, or fashion falsely'). · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To feign is to pretend to have or feel something that one does not actually have or feel.

To avoid an awkward conversation at the reunion, she feigned a phone call and stepped outside.

Worked Example

The poker player feigned disappointment at her cards, sighing dramatically, when in fact she was holding a winning hand.

Notice the subject here is a person deliberately putting on a false show of emotion -- feign is always about someone's own conscious choice to pretend, unlike "belie," where some detail or fact accidentally gives away the truth.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

pose: To pose is to pretend to be someone or something you are not — a con artist poses as a safety inspector. Feign points at feelings instead: you feign an emotion or a condition, not an identity. If the lie is about who you are, use pose; if it is about what you feel, use feign.

fake: Fake is the everyday, casual word for making something seem real when it is not — you can fake a signature, a permission slip, or a laugh. Feign is its formal cousin and applies almost only to feelings and conditions a person pretends to have, like feigned surprise or a feigned illness.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

reveal: to make an emotion or fact genuinely known

betray: to unintentionally show a true feeling one meant to hide

Where it sits · how fully the pretense is acted out — bluff → feign → simulate

bluff vs. feign: A bluff sits below feign in how fully it is acted out: a bluff is nothing but a bold claim, empty words meant to scare someone off, while to feign an emotion you must actually perform it with your face and voice.

simulate vs. feign: Simulate goes further than feign: feigning surprise takes only a quick false expression, while simulating an engine failure recreates the entire event in full, convincing detail.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — fei-/fic-

root — fei-/fic-: to shape, form, or fashion (often falsely) (Latin (fingere))

Put it together

Put it together: Feign traces back to the Latin verb fingere, 'to shape or fashion' -- often in the sense of shaping a false impression. To feign something is to 'fashion' a fake version of an emotion or condition.

Use the root in a new word: feint

Use the root in a new word: feint: The boxer threw a feint with his left hand to distract his opponent before landing a real punch with his right.

Root Check

Word Choice

Feign is always about a person's own deliberate act of pretending. Compare "belie," where some involuntary detail -- a tone, an expression -- contradicts the truth without anyone consciously acting. 'She feigned surprise' is a choice; 'her face belied her surprise' is an involuntary giveaway.
